items.originalTitle: Tokyo won’t fall as hard as Seoul or Taipei when the AI trade cools, says Japan Exchange Group CEO Hiromi Yamaji
items.author: Angelica Ang
items.title: Tokyo won’t fall as hard as Seoul or Taipei when the AI trade cools, says Japan Exchange Group CEO Hiromi Yamaji
items.summary: Global AI stocks sold off sharply over the past week, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO and tighter rules around semiconductor exports. Not even Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO on Thursday revived sentiment. Tech-heavy indices fell sharply: the Nasdaq 100 fell 9.1% last week, while the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index is down by 13% over the same period. Yet Hiromi Yamaji, CEO of the Japan Exchange Group (JPX), isn’t too worried about the tech turmoil hitting Japan too hard. “The weight of AI or semiconductor-related stocks in the TOPIX is only 11.3%… in the S&P 500 it’s 20%, in the Nasdaq100 it’s 27%, in Taiwan it’s 47%, and in Korea it’s 60%,” Yamaji tells Fortune . “If there is much less trading volume of AI-related stocks, then we will see some decrease in trading value, but the impact won’t be as much as in other markets.” The TOPIX index, which covers the broader Japanese equity market and was developed by JPX, fell 7% last week. Japan’s other benchmark index, the Nikkei 225, dropped by 8% over the same period. (The Nikkei 225, developed by Nikkei Inc., tracks a smaller number of large Japanese companies, including more tech manufacturing companies). Taiwan’s TAIEX index—where chipmaker TSMC makes up over 40% of the weight—crashed by 13% last week, prompting the island’s government to take measures against short-selling on Thursday to stabilize markets. Japanese equities hit historic highs in the summer of 2026 following a series of corporate governance reforms Yamaji launched, which were aimed at improving market transparency and fairness. The rules have strengthened rules regarding protection of minority shareholders and cross-shareholding within Japan’s sprawling conglomerates. Since April 2025, JPX has mandated that firms on its Prime Market board must give disclosures in both English and Japanese . Between 2024 and 2026, average trading volume on the Tokyo Stock Exchange more than doubled from 5.7 trillion yen ($35.9 billion) to 12 trillion yen ($75.5 billion). The amount of Japanese stocks bought by foreign investors also jumped from 5.4 trillion yen ($34 billion) in 2025 to 10.8 trillion yen ($68 billion) in the first ten months of 2026, according to JPX data. “We need to [undertake these reforms] in order to improve the quality of our listed products, but we have to get support from those listed companies as well,” Yamaji explains. “That takes time… [Many] Japanese traditional companies don’t like whatever we’re doing, like the corporate governance reforms.” The Japanese government has also worked to increasingly shift household cash into the stock market. In 2024, they revamped the Nippon Individual Savings Account (NISA) —a government tax-free investment program for Japanese residents—by introducing an unlimited tax-free period on dividends and investment gains and raising the annual investment limit to 3.6 million Japanese yen ($22,600). The number of NISA accounts jumped from 22.5 million in 2024 to over 31 million by September 2026. The total amount invested via these accounts increased from 31 trillion Japanese yen in 2023 to 88.4 trillion Japanese yen in 2026. In an August op-ed for International Banker, Yamaji noted that this growth was led by those under 50. In April, the JPX updated its request to listed companies to explain how they will start allocating more cash to growth, rather than just using surplus capital for share buybacks. Corporate share buybacks had reached a multi-year high in 2025, amounting to 22.3 trillion yen ($140.3 billion) . “Companies have to deliver results, that is, actual growth,” Yamaji says. “This is the more difficult stage since there’s no one-size-fits-all solution. Each company has to formulate their own plan based on their own unique situations.” The JPX also hopes to improve its appeal to non-Japanese companies. Currently, just five of the 3,884 firms listed on the TSE are foreign companies. The TSE launched the “ Asia start-up hub ” initiative in 2024 that helps Asian startups raise money and set up in Japan. Firms from ten economies across Asia—including Singapore, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Mongolia and the Philippines—have joined. Thus far, 26 firms, ranging from Vietnamese music start-up POPS to Taiwan-based Internet of Energy (IoE) platform NextDrive, have enrolled in JPX’s incubator program. “It’s an ecosystem to support Asian start-ups to come to Japan, not only for the TSE listing, but also to grow their own businesses by using the Japanese market as an incubator,” Yamaji says. “The Japanese economy is big enough for them to grow.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.summary: How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties. The same carbon atoms, for example, can form diamond and graphite depending on how they are arranged, giving rise to materials with vastly different chemical and physical properties. Now, researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a new crystal structure of silver with unusually high chemical reactivity. The findings, published in Nano Letters, could open new avenues for exploring materials with desirable properties.

items.originalTitle: CT families deserve to see every home for sale
items.author: Jorge Cabrera
items.title: CT families deserve to see every home for sale
items.summary: The families I meet across Connecticut aren’t asking for much. Among other things, they all want a fair shot at buying a home, not a bidding war over a home they never knew they lost, or missing out on a house that sold before it ever hit the market. As of October 1, Connecticut law now says they deserve better than that. State Sen. Jorge Cabrera " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Jorge-Cabrera-e1794840340454.png" src="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Jorge-Cabrera-e1794840340454.png" alt="" class="wp-image-1104745" style="width:169px;height:auto"/> State Sen. Jorge Cabrera As chair of the Senate’s Insurance and Real Estate Committee, I helped write and steer through the legislature Senate Bill 340 , which Gov. Ned Lamont signed into law earlier this year. Now, real estate listings in Connecticut default to what’s called public marketing: a home is shown to the broadest possible pool of buyers, unless the seller signs a specific form acknowledging what they’re giving up by keeping it private. I spent more than two decades as a union organizer before I came to the legislature, fighting for workers who too often got the short end of a deal that they didn’t fully understand. This new law follows that same principle: people deserve to know what they’re agreeing to before they sign away something valuable — in this case, transparency, the very thing that determines whether a family gets a fair shot at a home and whether a seller gets a fair price for it. Here’s the problem that S.B. 340 solves. In recent years, more agents and brokerages have quietly marketed homes only within their own networks — sometimes called “private listings” or “pocket listings” by the industry — rather than putting them on the open market where everyone can see them. The financial incentive is obvious: when a brokerage controls both sides of the transaction, it collects the full commission. For the brokerage, that’s a win. For a family who never knew the house even existed, it’s something else entirely. We’re in the middle of a housing supply crisis, and Connecticut simply doesn’t have enough homes for the people who want to live here. Private listings make that problem worse. When a home is marketed only inside a brokerage’s private network, it’s invisible to most buyers, and an invisible home might as well not exist. It is, in effect, a manufactured scarcity on top of real housing scarcity, and it distorts the very market mechanism that we’re all counting on to help solve the affordability crisis. More supply only helps if buyers can actually see what’s for sale. S.B. 340 isn’t a ban on private sales. If a homeowner genuinely wants to keep a sale quiet, either for privacy, for a family transfer, or for any reason, they still can. What the new law requires is that they be told, clearly and in writing, what that choice will cost them. That’s the same basic consumer protection we already expect in almost every other major purchase we make. Connecticut’s version of this law is among the strongest in the country. It closes a loophole that allowed agents to quietly circulate listings by email within their own networks before ever opening them to the public — a practice that preserved the appearance of compliance while undermining the spirit of open marketing. It also ensures that any platform used to market a home can’t restrict access to benefit a single brokerage’s bottom line. We didn’t get here alone. Washington and Wisconsin moved first; New York has now passed its own version. Legislators from both parties have backed these bills, because making sure buyers can see what’s for sale isn’t a partisan question — it’s a basic fairness question. But Connecticut’s law sets a higher bar than what came before it, and that matters. The families I represent didn’t create this crisis. They deserve a law that doesn’t make it worse — and now they have one. State Sen. Jorge Cabrera represents the 17th State Senate District, covering Ansonia, Beacon Falls, Bethany, Derby, Hamden, Naugatuck and Woodbridge. He is Senate Chair of the Insurance and Real Estate Committee.

items.originalTitle: CT must now confront the costs of past PURA decisions
items.author: Marcelo Assis
items.title: CT must now confront the costs of past PURA decisions
items.summary: The men and women I represent at United Steelworkers Local 12000 work every day on Southern Connecticut Gas’s natural gas system, maintaining pipes, responding when problems arise and performing the work necessary to keep energy flowing safely and reliably to Connecticut homes and businesses. That gives our members a practical perspective on energy regulation. Decisions made in hearing rooms and regulatory proceedings can seem far removed from the field, but over time they shape the work our crews can plan, the infrastructure they maintain and the ability of the system to serve customers and communities. Under the previous leadership of PURA, one approach to limiting pressure on customer bills was to restrict or defer costs, including investments in the system. While that may have provided some near-term relief, it could not defer the physical needs of the system itself. Infrastructure continued to age, maintenance and replacement work remained necessary, and employees still had to keep the system operating safely and reliably. Deferring that work did not eliminate the need; it allowed projects to accumulate, making future planning more difficult and increasing the risk that routine infrastructure needs become larger, more complex challenges over time. The new leadership at PURA inherited many of the challenges created by that approach. The current commissioners did not make those decisions, and they should not be asked to defend them. But they now have an opportunity to learn from that experience and establish a more predictable approach to the investments required to maintain the system over the long term. Our members understand why that matters. Maintaining a gas system safely requires more than responding to the needs we can see today. Utilities and their workers need to look ahead, identify infrastructure that will need attention, anticipate where additional capacity may be required and build the skilled workforce necessary to perform that work. When there is not a predictable approach to forward capital investment, that planning becomes much harder. Projects can be delayed or reprioritized, workforce needs become more difficult to anticipate, and decisions about hiring, training and developing the next generation of skilled workers become more uncertain. This is specialized work, and an experienced workforce cannot be created overnight. Maintaining those skills requires a steady and responsible pipeline of work. The consequences also reach the infrastructure itself. Deferring maintenance or replacement does not stop pipes from aging or equipment from requiring attention. Instead, work that can be planned and performed methodically today can become more difficult to manage later. Our members would rather address infrastructure needs at a steady, responsible pace than continually push work forward until the need becomes more urgent. That same need to plan ahead applies to the communities we serve. Across Connecticut, communities are looking to add housing, support local businesses and attract new employers and skilled workers. Reliable energy infrastructure is one part of the foundation needed to support that growth. When parts of the gas system become constrained, the implications can extend beyond the utility. Limited capacity can make it more difficult to connect new customers, accommodate business expansion or support development in communities that are trying to grow. Planning ahead can help address emerging constraints before infrastructure becomes an obstacle to those opportunities. That is why the distinction between the previous PURA and the PURA Connecticut has today matters so much. The lesson from the past is not that regulators should approve every investment a utility proposes. Regulators should scrutinize spending, demand accountability and make sure customers receive value for what they pay. But scrutiny and predictability can coexist. A strong regulatory system can protect customers while providing enough visibility for utilities to plan necessary work, for employees to develop and maintain specialized skills, and for communities to know that infrastructure will be capable of supporting their future needs. Connecticut cannot undo the regulatory decisions that brought us here, and the current commissioners should not be blamed for circumstances they inherited. What the new PURA can do is take a different approach going forward, one that recognizes that delaying investment does not delay the needs of the system. For our members, that is ultimately what this debate is about. A more predictable approach to forward investment allows necessary work to proceed at a responsible pace, supports the skilled workforce needed to perform it and helps prevent infrastructure constraints from becoming larger challenges for customers and communities. The new PURA inherited a difficult situation. It also inherited an opportunity to build something better: a regulatory approach that protects affordability while providing the consistency needed to maintain a safe, reliable system and support Connecticut communities for years to come. Marcelo Assis is President of the United Steelworkers Local 12000 & 12000-1.
